Foundations of LLM Post-Training in Changing Environments

Diverse Alternative Reasoning Traces
for Hard Math Problems

Lukas Aichberger ††thanks: Johannes Kepler University Linz (Work done during an internship at Apple Inc.)    Adam Goliński ††thanks: Apple Inc. Correspondence to: Sinead Williamson <sa_williamson@apple.com>    Arno Blaas 22footnotemark: 2    Arwen Bradley 22footnotemark: 2    Jacob Springer ††thanks: Carnegie Mellon University (Work done during an internship at Apple Inc.) Affiliation: Mehrdad Farajtabar22footnotemark: 2 , Michael Kirchhof22footnotemark: 2 , Sinead Williamson22footnotemark: 2
Abstract

Post-training large language models (LLMs) for mathematical reasoning often relies on accepted traces whose final answers pass a verifier. For hard math problems, however, such traces can be rare under independent Monte Carlo (MC) sampling. To address this, we propose Diverse Alternative Reasoning Traces (DART), a trace-mining method that starts from a rejected trace, decomposes it into reasoning steps, and ranks them by position-weighted uncertainty. It then generates deliberately distinct alternative candidates for highly ranked steps using reference-answer guidance and a meta-thought before completing the resulting traces. On greedy-unsolved DeepMath-103K problems, DART recovers 37% more problems than MC sampling at a matched number of generated traces. Its estimated generation cost per recovered problem is nearly identical, while its cost per accepted trace is 30% lower. Post-training Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on traces mined by DART achieves the highest point estimate in five of six evaluations across MATH-500 and AIME benchmarks. These results demonstrate that revisiting rejected traces with DART can expand problem coverage and provide effective post-training data.

1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly employed in tasks that require complex, multi-step problem solving (Srivastava et al., 2023). One such task is mathematical reasoning, where prompting LLMs to generate intermediate reasoning steps rather than directly predicting the final answer has been shown to substantially improve their problem-solving performance (Wei et al., 2022).

To further improve their reasoning capabilities, LLMs are commonly post-trained on reasoning traces (Lightman et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024; Muennighoff et al., 2025). Since high-quality traces are generally difficult to obtain at scale, a common approach is to generate them from the model itself using Monte Carlo (MC) sampling at nonzero temperature. The generated traces can then be evaluated using verifiable rewards, based on whether the final answer to a mathematical problem matches a known reference answer, and subsequently used for post-training (Zelikman et al., 2022; Guo et al., 2025). We refer to traces as accepted if they pass the verifier and rejected otherwise.

A key limitation is that this approach provides no post-training data for problems where MC sampling fails to generate an accepted trace (Yu et al., 2025b; Zheng et al., 2025; Kirk et al., 2024; Cui et al., 2025), which is often the case for the hard mathematical problems we consider (Section 4). Moreover, repeated sampling may produce similar traces, leaving alternative reasoning strategies unexplored. This turns trace generation into a question of problem coverage. A problem contributes post-training data only if the model generates at least one accepted trace. This creates a model-dependent data collection process that can underrepresent problems for which the model has a low probability of generating an accepted trace.

Let q𝜽​(𝐱)q_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}) be the success probability of a fixed decoding policy on problem 𝐱\mathbf{x}. With kk independent traces from MC sampling, the probability of obtaining at least one accepted trace is

1−(1−q𝜽​(𝐱))k.1-\bigl(1-q_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{x})\bigr)^{k}. (1)

When k​q𝜽​(𝐱)≪1k\,q_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{x})\ll 1, Equation 1 is approximately k​q𝜽​(𝐱)k\,q_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}), so MC sampling leaves many low-q𝜽q_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} problems without an accepted trace at practical kk (Yu et al., 2025b; Zheng et al., 2025). Moreover, MC sampling starts each attempt from scratch, without leveraging the structure of previous failed attempts or controlling which local decision to change.

To address this, we argue that low-probability regions should be explored more deliberately by increasing diversity in the traces. We propose Diverse Alternative Reasoning Traces (DART), a trace-mining method for this setting. Starting from a rejected trace generated by an LLM, DART decomposes the trace into reasoning steps, ranks these steps by position-weighted uncertainty, and selects uncertain reasoning steps for branching. At a selected reasoning step, DART leverages the model’s own reasoning capabilities to propose a conceptually distinct alternative candidate conditioned on the preceding steps, the selected step, and the reference answer, with a meta-thought guiding the alternative strategy. This prompts the model to depart from the original greedy trace. The model then greedily completes the trace from this alternative candidate onward (see Figure 1). We evaluate DART through component analyses on MATH-500 (Section 2), problem coverage and generation cost on two mining datasets (Section 4), and subsequent post-training (Section 5).

Across multiple mathematical reasoning datasets, DART recovers problems missed by full-trace MC sampling. Ablations show that removing reference-answer guidance still yields improved problem coverage over matched step-level MC sampling. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on the resulting training corpora also yields higher downstream point estimates than MC sampling. Together, these findings support targeted exploration of rejected traces as a practical approach to collecting post-training data.

Our main findings are:

  • •

    At a matched number of completed traces, DART recovers more problems than MC sampling, with the largest gains on the hardest problems, reaching up to 2×2\times higher problem coverage (Figure 4).

  • •

    Position-weighted greedy negative log-likelihood (G-NLLPOS{}_{\texttt{POS}}) reduces the mean number of alternative candidates required to obtain an accepted trace by about 40% relative to random selection on problems with both accepted and rejected completed traces (Figure 2).

  • •

    DART recovers 37% more problems and generates 45% more accepted traces per recovered problem than MC sampling, yielding nearly twice as many accepted traces at a 30% lower estimated generation cost per accepted trace, despite a 39% higher cost per attempted problem (Figure 5).

  • •

    In post-training evaluations, DART achieves up to 5 percentage points higher Greedy ∪\cup pass@32 accuracy than MC sampling and the highest point estimate in five of six evaluations (Table 1).

2 Method

Let the dataset 𝒟={(𝐱n,𝐚n)}n=1N\mathcal{D}=\{(\mathbf{x}_{n},\mathbf{a}_{n})\}_{n=1}^{N} contain problems and reference answers, and let p𝜽p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} denote a language model used to propose and complete traces. For each problem 𝐱\mathbf{x}, we first greedily generate a trace 𝐭\mathbf{t} using the chain-of-thought (CoT) instruction 𝐩CoT=\mathbf{p}_{\texttt{CoT}}= “Let’s think step by step and output the final answer within \boxed{}”. We then verify its final answer against the reference answer 𝐚\mathbf{a} using Math-Verify, denoted by v⁡(𝐭,𝐚)∈{0,1}\smash{v(\mathbf{t},\mathbf{a})\in\{0,1\}}11 1 https://github.com/huggingface/Math-Verify, treating traces that do not terminate normally as rejected. We note that although this outcome verifier does not establish the validity of every intermediate reasoning step, it provides an automated signal for identifying traces that arrive at the correct final answer (Cobbe et al., 2021; Lightman et al., 2024).

An accepted greedy trace is retained directly; a rejected greedy trace is processed through reasoning step decomposition, reasoning step selection, and reasoning step diversity sampling (Figure 1).

For a selected position jj and alternative candidate index rr, the completed trace has the form

𝐭ALTj,r=𝐬<j∥𝐬ALTj,r∥𝐜j,r,\mathbf{t}^{j,r}_{\texttt{ALT}}=\mathbf{s}^{<j}\mathbin{\|}\mathbf{s}^{j,r}_{\texttt{ALT}}\mathbin{\|}\mathbf{c}^{j,r}, (2)

where ∥\| denotes concatenation. The suffix 𝐬>j\mathbf{s}^{>j} of the rejected trace is discarded, allowing the alternative candidate to change subsequent reasoning rather than reconnecting to the original trace.

Unlike full-trace MC sampling, which independently samples new traces from p𝜽p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}, DART reuses the prefix 𝐬<j\mathbf{s}^{<j} and generates a meta-thought, the alternative candidate 𝐬ALTj,r\smash{\mathbf{s}^{j,r}_{\texttt{ALT}}}, and the subsequent continuation 𝐜j,r\mathbf{c}^{j,r} with p𝜽p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}. This avoids regenerating the shared prefix, although sampling 𝐬ALTj,r\smash{\mathbf{s}^{j,r}_{\texttt{ALT}}} incurs additional compute due to reasoning step diversity sampling. We analyze this trade-off in Section 4.

Consequently, the completed traces constructed by DART are not independent samples from p𝜽p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} under the original decoding policy. Instead, our method conditions on a previous rejected trace and targets uncertain reasoning steps at which an alternative candidate may lead to a different final answer. By deliberately departing from the original decoding policy, DART aims to improve problem coverage, particularly for problems with low q𝜽​(𝐱)q_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}). This locally induced shift in the sampling distribution is compatible with our post-training setup, where the training objective does not require on-policy sampling. We therefore retain every accepted trace for post-training. We measure problem coverage as the number of problems with at least one accepted trace. A problem is greedy-solved if its greedy trace is accepted and greedy-unsolved otherwise. Recovering a greedy-unsolved problem means obtaining an accepted alternative trace. We next detail the three stages used to construct these traces.

2.1 Reasoning step decomposition

To decompose a trace 𝐭\mathbf{t} into individual reasoning steps, one can use rule-based delimiters, such as line breaks (Wan et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024b; Xie et al., 2024; Tian et al., 2024). However, such heuristics can fail to capture meaningful reasoning step boundaries. Multi-line sentences may be split into incomplete steps, while single lines containing multiple sentences may conflate distinct steps.

To address this, we use the language model itself to predict reasoning step boundaries. Specifically, we first split 𝐭\mathbf{t} deterministically at sentence-final punctuation and line breaks to obtain text fragments. We then use a reasoning step decomposition prompt 𝐩AUG\mathbf{p}_{\texttt{AUG}} that guides the model to predict explicit [STEP] markers between text fragments. The model generates boundary decisions while the trace itself is teacher-forced. The model therefore classifies boundaries without regenerating or editing the trace. Based on these markers, 𝐭\mathbf{t} is deterministically decomposed into reasoning steps {𝐬j}j=1J⁡(𝐭)\smash{\{\mathbf{s}^{j}\}_{j=1}^{J(\mathbf{t})}}, where J⁡(𝐭)\smash{J(\mathbf{t})} is trace-dependent. This procedure preserves the original trace while allowing boundaries to depend on context (see Appendix A for 𝐩AUG\mathbf{p}_{\texttt{AUG}} and examples).

Reasoning step decomposition adds only a small generation cost. The trace is teacher-forced, so each boundary decision decodes a single token, and the key-value (KV) cache of the annotated prefix can be reused across consecutive decisions. Decisions are batched across traces, only rejected greedy traces are decomposed, and decomposition during trace mining stops after ten closed reasoning steps (Appendix A). Since decomposition only places boundaries rather than generating reasoning, it need not use the policy model p𝜽p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}. A smaller model could further reduce this cost, but we leave this to future work.

2.2 Reasoning step selection

Generating alternative candidates for all reasoning steps {𝐬j}j=1J⁡(𝐭)\smash{\{\mathbf{s}^{j}\}_{j=1}^{J(\mathbf{t})}} would make the number of alternative candidates scale with trace length and become computationally expensive for long traces. We therefore select step positions jj that are most likely to yield a different reasoning strategy and, in turn, a different final answer. We consider several selection strategies guided by two main intuitions:(i) uncertain steps are promising to revisit, and (ii) alternative reasoning strategies are more likely to emerge earlier in the trace.

Among these strategies, the position-weighted G-NLL (Aichberger et al., 2026) of each reasoning step (G-NLLPOS{}_{\texttt{POS}}) performs best. Given 𝐬j\mathbf{s}^{j}, it is defined as

u(𝐬j)=−1j∑i=1|𝐬j|logp𝜽(sij∣𝐱,𝐬<j,𝐬<ij).u(\mathbf{s}^{j})=-\ \frac{1}{j}\sum_{i=1}^{|\mathbf{s}^{j}|}\log p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\left(s_{i}^{j}\mid\mathbf{x},\mathbf{s}^{<j},\mathbf{s}_{<i}^{j}\right). (3)

We select steps with the largest scores. Dividing by jj favors early uncertain steps, where replacing the original reasoning step can redirect a larger portion of the remaining trace. We compare rankings on greedy-unsolved MATH-500 problems with both accepted and rejected completed traces, the only problems on which the ranking can change the rank of the first accepted trace (125 problems; Figure 2, Appendix B). On this subset, G-NLLPOS{}_{\texttt{POS}} places the first accepted trace at a mean rank slightly below four, compared with nearly seven under random selection, a reduction of about 40%. This measures ranking effectiveness within the recorded sets of completed traces, rather than overall search cost across all greedy-unsolved problems. All uncertainty- and position-based scores yield lower mean ranks than random selection and perform similarly, indicating that the benefit of targeted selection is robust to the choice of score, while self-reported confidence performs slightly worse. We use the best-performing score, G-NLLPOS{}_{\texttt{POS}}, throughout the remaining experiments.

2.3 Reasoning step diversity sampling

Once we have selected a reasoning step 𝐬j\mathbf{s}^{j}, we aim to generate an alternative candidate 𝐬ALTj,r\mathbf{s}^{j,r}_{\texttt{ALT}} that follows a different reasoning strategy. A simple baseline is step-level MC sampling, which samples from p𝜽(⋅∣𝐱,𝐬<j)p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{x},\mathbf{s}^{<j}) at temperature TT. While this introduces stochasticity, it does not condition on the original step 𝐬j\mathbf{s}^{j} and therefore cannot explicitly encourage the alternative candidate to differ from it.

We thus introduce a diversity prompt 𝐩DIV\mathbf{p}_{\texttt{DIV}} that includes 𝐬j\mathbf{s}^{j} as contrastive context and instructs the model to construct an alternative candidate based on a fundamentally different reasoning strategy. The alternative candidate should form a single self-contained reasoning step, continue the retained prefix 𝐬<j\mathbf{s}^{<j} in the same format and style, replace 𝐬j\mathbf{s}^{j} without repeating or referring back to it, and offer a non-obvious perspective that 𝐬j\mathbf{s}^{j} does not anticipate (Appendix C). Alternative candidates are generated sequentially: for alternative candidate rr, the diversity prompt includes the selected reasoning step and all earlier alternative candidates. This changes the context even under greedy decoding, encouraging distinct alternative candidates without guaranteeing semantic diversity.

In DART (w/ sol, w/ rsn), the prompt additionally provides the reference answer 𝐚\mathbf{a}, with instructions not to reveal it, and asks the model to first generate a meta-thought about a suitable alternative strategy (Meta-Thought in Figure 1). Both components only shape the proposal. The meta-thought is discarded, and the continuation 𝐜j,r\mathbf{c}^{j,r} is greedily generated from 𝐬<j∥𝐬ALTj,r\mathbf{s}^{<j}\mathbin{\|}\mathbf{s}^{j,r}_{\texttt{ALT}} under the original instruction 𝐩CoT\mathbf{p}_{\texttt{CoT}}, without access to 𝐩DIV\mathbf{p}_{\texttt{DIV}}, 𝐚\mathbf{a}, or the meta-thought. Reference-answer guidance therefore enters the completed trace only through the alternative candidate. We ablate these two components in a 2×22\times 2 comparison, removing reference-answer guidance, the meta-thought, or both (Figure 3).

The diversity prompt 𝐩DIV\mathbf{p}_{\texttt{DIV}} encourages a qualitative change in reasoning strategy rather than optimizing an explicit semantic-distance objective. We therefore assess its effectiveness through problem coverage. Figure 3 compares DART and its three ablations (blue) on MATH-500 using Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Grattafiori et al., 2024; Lightman et al., 2024). Our primary baseline, step-level MC sampling with greedy continuation (red), samples an alternative candidate at T=1T=1 and continues greedily like DART, so that the comparison isolates the proposal procedure at a matched completed-trace budget. Removing both reference-answer guidance and the meta-thought gives the closest ablation to this baseline. We also compare against step-level MC sampling with sampled continuation (dark green), which samples both at T=1T=1, and full-trace MC sampling (light green), which generates each trace from scratch.

Among problems with normally terminated greedy traces, DART recovers 170 problems at the largest evaluated step-level budget, compared with 148 for step-level MC sampling with greedy continuation, about 15% more recoveries. The ablations without reference-answer guidance recover 158 problems without a meta-thought and 155 with one, showing that reference-answer guidance helps but is not necessary for improved recovery.

With one to four alternative candidates per selected reasoning step, DART covers 350, 373, 386, and 394 problems (including 224 greedy-solved problems), versus 332, 356, 365, and 372 for step-level MC sampling with greedy continuation (Figure 6). At the largest budget, its problem coverage also exceeds that of full-trace MC sampling with 51 traces. Some DART recoveries are missed even by full-trace MC sampling with 1,024 traces, illustrating complementary problem coverage (Section C.3). Algorithm 1 brings the three stages together into the complete trace-mining procedure.

3 Related work

Diverse reasoning and verified post-training.

Chain-of-thought prompting elicits intermediate reasoning (Wei et al., 2022), and self-consistency samples multiple traces and aggregates their answers (Wang et al., 2023). Other methods diversify decompositions, demonstrations, or solution paths at inference or during training (Zhou et al., 2023; Press et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023; Li et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2025a; Dokmeci et al., 2025). Rejection fine-tuning and ReST retain accepted model-generated traces for subsequent learning (Yuan et al., 2023; Gulcehre et al., 2023). STaR additionally regenerates rejected traces conditioned on the reference answer, then fine-tunes on accepted traces and repeats generation, combining reference-answer guidance during data acquisition with iterative model improvement (Zelikman et al., 2022). Related work improves trace selection with verifiers or process supervision (Hosseini et al., 2024; Lightman et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024; Luo et al., 2024), or optimizes directly against verifiable rewards (Shao et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025b). DART targets the preceding data-acquisition step. It shares STaR’s reference-answer guidance, but proposes a local alternative candidate from a rejected trace rather than regenerating the full trace. The resulting accepted traces can feed standard supervised or reinforcement-learning objectives.

Guided search.

Tree-of-Thoughts and RAP organize reasoning as search over intermediate states (Yao et al., 2023; Hao et al., 2023). Subsequent systems combine tree search with learned critics, process rewards, self-training, or preference optimization (Wan et al., 2024; Tian et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025; Guan et al., 2025). For example, ReST-MCTS* alternates process-reward-guided search with training of both the policy and process reward model (Zhang et al., 2024b). Contract-checked graph editing instead recombines partial traces under structural and deterministic checks (Li and Cao, 2026). Uncertainty-guided methods use local uncertainty to decide where to branch (Mo and Xin, 2024; Li et al., 2026). Entropy-Gated Branching branches only at high-uncertainty steps and prunes expansions with a lightweight verifier, while ROSE uses semantic entropy to allocate branches within reinforcement learning (Li et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026). DART builds on this line of work but addresses a complementary question: how to propose an alternative candidate once a reasoning step is selected. The selected reasoning step serves as contrastive context for the proposal, while acceptance depends only on the completed trace’s final answer. This requires neither learned step rewards nor critic updates. Our step-level comparisons fix the model, verifier, problems, and completed-trace budget. They therefore study the proposal mechanism rather than compare complete search systems that also introduce critics, backups, or new training objectives.

Reflection and correction.

Self-Refine uses the same model to generate feedback and iteratively revise a response (Madaan et al., 2023). Reflexion stores linguistic feedback across attempts (Shinn et al., 2023). Other methods learn to critique, correct, or check generated responses (Saunders et al., 2022; Welleck et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2024a; Wang et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025). DART instead retains the prefix before a selected reasoning step, replaces that reasoning step, and discards the original suffix. Its meta-thought guides this local proposal without asserting that the selected reasoning step is the first error. Only the resulting accepted trace, not the meta-thought or rejected trace, is used for SFT.

4 Mining traces with DART

The MATH-500 component analyses examine where to branch and how to construct alternative candidates. We now evaluate whether the complete DART procedure expands problem coverage on larger mining datasets and how this affects generation cost. We compare it with full-trace MC sampling, hereafter MC sampling, on the mining datasets DeepMath-103K (He et al., 2025) and OpenMathInstruct-2 (Toshniwal et al., 2025), using Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct to make both the 512-trace difficulty analysis and post-training tractable.

Evaluation unit and metric.

Throughout this section, we evaluate only greedy-unsolved problems. At a budget of kk completed traces per problem, problem coverage is the number of recovered problems, each with at least one accepted trace. For MC sampling before stratification, the per-problem recovery probability is given by Equation 1. Problem coverage counts a recovered problem once, irrespective of how many accepted traces it yields, and therefore does not measure semantic diversity among traces. It thus measures how many previously uncovered problems contribute post-training data.

Model-adjusted difficulty.

To localize the gains, we stratify problems by q𝜽​(𝐱)q_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}) from Section 1. Human-oriented labels need not align with this model-dependent quantity (Figure 7 in Appendix D). For each pair (𝐱,𝐚)(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{a}), we estimate q𝜽​(𝐱)q_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}) from a pool of 512 independent traces generated by MC sampling at T=1T=1,

q^(𝐱)=1512∑ℓ=1512v(𝐭ℓ,𝐚),𝐭ℓ∼p𝜽(⋅∣𝐱;T=1).\widehat{q}(\mathbf{x})=\frac{1}{512}\sum_{\ell=1}^{512}v(\mathbf{t}^{\ell},\mathbf{a}),\qquad\mathbf{t}^{\ell}\sim p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{x};T=1). (4)

Using the fixed ranges in Appendix D, we form eight strata of up to 255 greedy-unsolved problems per dataset, ordered from easiest to hardest. This subsampling does not affect the generated traces or the training corpora (Section 5). The displayed results of MC sampling use traces from this same 512-trace pool, so stratification and evaluation are not independent. In particular, by construction, MC sampling recovers no problem with q^​(𝐱)=0\widehat{q}(\mathbf{x})=0. The strata describe empirical sampling difficulty, so zero observed successes does not imply zero underlying success probability.

Matched completed-trace budget.

MC sampling draws k∈{1,2,4}k\in\{1,2,4\} independent full traces per problem at T=1T=1. DART uses the same completed-trace budget kk, distributing it across selected reasoning steps and alternative candidates. At k=2k=2, we evaluate both two alternative candidates for one selected reasoning step and one alternative candidate for each of two selected reasoning steps, separating the benefit of exploring multiple alternative candidates at a single step from intervening at multiple steps. This design allows each DART configuration to be compared directly with MC sampling at the same number of completed traces.

Results.

Figure 4 shows that DART consistently achieves higher aggregate problem coverage than MC sampling across all displayed budget allocations on both datasets, with results for larger budgets provided in Figures 8 and 9 (Appendix D). Increasing the completed-trace budget further improves coverage: both k=2k=2 allocations outperform k=1k=1, while generating two alternative candidates at each of two selected reasoning steps (k=4k=4) achieves the highest coverage. These results support exploring multiple alternative candidates both within and across reasoning steps.

Notably, DART also recovers problems in the hardest strata. The methods recover partially overlapping sets of problems, with some recovered exclusively by DART and others exclusively by MC sampling. Together, these findings highlight that targeted generation of alternative candidates recovers problems that are difficult to reach through independent sampling, while suggesting that the two approaches could be combined to further expand problem coverage.

Generation-cost analysis.

The primary comparison controls for the number of completed traces but not differences in computational cost. We therefore analyze generation cost (Figure 5) on greedy-unsolved problems from DeepMath-103K. MC sampling generates eight full traces per problem at T=1T=1. With a budget of up to eight completed traces, DART selects up to four reasoning steps and generates two alternative candidates per step. For each completed trace, the model first generates a meta-thought and alternative candidate at T=0T=0, followed by a greedy continuation. This yields up to 49,600 completed traces for DART and MC sampling. Both methods use the same 4,096-token completion allowance. For DART, retained prefixes and alternative candidates count toward this allowance, with retained-prefix KV caches being reused to avoid redundant computation.

We estimate generation FLOPs accounting for differences in sequence length and prefix reuse. The estimate includes alternative candidate generation and trace completion but excludes reasoning step decomposition, the shared initial greedy attempt, and non-generation overhead. It therefore does not measure end-to-end runtime (see Appendix E for details).

Coverage and cost.

Figure 5 shows that DART recovers 2,971 of 6,200 problems (48%), compared with 2,168 (35%) for MC sampling, corresponding to 37% more recovered problems. This increased coverage comes at a 39% higher estimated generation cost per attempted problem. However, the cost per recovered problem remains nearly unchanged, while the cost per accepted trace decreases by 30% because DART produces almost twice as many accepted traces. These results demonstrate that targeted exploration can substantially improve both problem recovery and accepted-trace yield without a proportional increase in estimated generation cost. In particular, the additional computation required to construct alternative candidates is effectively offset by improved problem coverage, allowing DART to recover substantially more problems at nearly the same estimated generation cost per recovered problem.

Explaining the cost trade-off.

The higher cost per attempted problem can be attributed primarily to the number of processed tokens. Projection and MLP operations account for approximately 88% and 91% of the estimated FLOPs for MC sampling and DART, respectively. DART processes 43% more uncached prompt and generated tokens than MC sampling, as each completed trace involves a diversity prompt and a meta-thought. However, it requires only 9% more causal token pairs, since reusing retained-prefix KV caches avoids recomputing attention over the shared prefix (Table 2).

The higher accepted-trace yield reflects two effects. DART recovers 1.37×1.37\times as many problems as MC sampling and yields 2.672.67 accepted traces per recovered problem, compared with 1.841.84 for MC sampling (Table 2), a further 1.45×1.45\times increase. Together, these factors explain the nearly twofold increase in accepted traces. Although the accepted traces are not semantically deduplicated, DART provides both broader problem coverage and more accepted reasoning traces per recovered problem for subsequent post-training.

5 Post-training on mined DART traces

We next evaluate the downstream value of traces mined by DART through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. We mine separate training corpora from 8k problems drawn from DeepMath-103K (He et al., 2025) and 16k problems drawn from OpenMathInstruct-2 (Toshniwal et al., 2025). Within each mining dataset, SFT on the training corpus obtained from each of the following mining methods starts from the same base checkpoint and uses the same SFT recipe and random seed:

  • •

    Greedy: All accepted greedy traces. This baseline training corpus is included in every other training corpus.

  • •

    MC sampling: Eight independent full traces at T=1T=1 for each rejected greedy trace, representing standard rejection sampling through repeated stochastic generation.

  • •

    STaR: One rationalization with reference-answer guidance for each rejected greedy trace, using the reference answer to elicit an accepted trace (Zelikman et al., 2022).

  • •

    RFT: Eight full traces at T=1T=1 with reference-answer guidance for each rejected greedy trace, combining rejection sampling with access to the reference answer (Yuan et al., 2023).

  • •

    DART: Two alternative candidates at each of up to four selected reasoning steps, followed by greedy continuation, yielding up to eight completed traces per rejected greedy trace.

STaR and RFT denote adapted mining baselines. Both receive the reference answer, as does DART. For DART, the meta-thought guides the proposal of an alternative candidate but is excluded from the training corpus. Each mining method retains only accepted traces. The resulting training corpora are not matched in examples or tokens because the mining methods recover different problems and yield different numbers of accepted traces. This end-to-end comparison evaluates the practical value of each mining method through downstream performance after SFT on its training corpus. With a fixed two-epoch SFT recipe, this comparison captures the combined benefits of the generated training corpora in terms of problem coverage, corpus size, and corpus composition, including the resulting differences in training volume.

Training and evaluation prompts.

For SFT, each accepted trace is paired only with the original problem 𝐱\mathbf{x} and CoT instruction 𝐩CoT\mathbf{p}_{\texttt{CoT}}, excluding all mining-specific guidance. Evaluation uses the same task prompt and likewise provides neither the reference answer 𝐚\mathbf{a} nor the rejected trace, alternative candidate, or meta-thought. The reference answer aa is used only for verification. Thus, the additional information available during mining serves exclusively to construct the training corpora and is unavailable to the fine-tuned model at inference time. The evaluation therefore measures generation under the original task setting.

Evaluation.

We report Greedy ∪\cup pass@32 accuracy (Table 1), counting a problem as solved if either a separate greedy trace or at least one of 32 stochastic traces is accepted. This metric captures both the model’s default greedy behavior and accepted traces obtainable through sampling, making it particularly relevant when greedy decoding alone may not yield an accepted trace. All models are evaluated using the same decoding, verification, and trace-resampling procedures to ensure consistent comparisons. We report the best-performing checkpoint for each model on each evaluation set. The uncertainty intervals reflect only resampling of the recorded trace pools, excluding training-seed variability and checkpoint-selection uncertainty. See Appendix F for the full training and evaluation protocol.

Results.

Across MATH-500 (Lightman et al., 2024) and AIME (Mathematical Association of America, 2022), DART achieves a higher point estimate than MC sampling in all six combinations of mining dataset and evaluation set (Table 1). Overall, DART ranks first in five of six evaluations, including all four AIME evaluations, with STaR only slightly outperforming it on MATH-500 after OpenMathInstruct-2 training. MATH-500 was used to develop the diversity prompt and reasoning step selection rule, while AIME informed neither choice. The AIME results therefore extend the evaluation beyond the benchmark used for method development, although AIME scores were used for checkpoint selection. Figure 10 in Appendix F additionally reports Greedy ∪\cup pass@kk curves, including cross-set evaluation of checkpoints selected on a single evaluation set.

STaR and RFT provide baselines with reference-answer guidance during mining. DART exceeds RFT in all six settings and STaR in five, showing favorable downstream point estimates against these baselines as well. Together, these results support targeted trace mining as an effective way to obtain post-training data.

6 Limitations

DART uses the reference answer when constructing alternative candidates, making it primarily suited to trace mining for post-training rather than test-time reasoning. However, ablations without reference-answer guidance still outperform matched step-level MC sampling (Figure 3). We verify final-answer correctness and evaluate exploration through problem coverage, which directly aligns with our objective of mining accepted traces. While these measures do not guarantee the validity of every intermediate reasoning step, this limitation is common to outcome-based verification approaches.

Our main coverage comparison controls for the number of completed traces, while a dedicated generation-cost analysis separately characterizes the compute trade-off at one representative operating point. The FLOP estimate excludes reasoning step decomposition and does not measure runtime. The post-training comparison evaluates complete mining methods, where corpus size, composition, and training volume vary together. This reflects the intended use of DART, where both broader problem coverage and a higher yield of accepted traces contribute to the value of the mined training corpus.

The empirical evaluation focuses primarily on one model and mathematical reasoning. While MATH-500 informed method development, the results on AIME extend the evaluation beyond this benchmark. Post-training uses one seed and evaluation-set checkpoint selection, and exact-string deduplication cannot exclude near-duplicate contamination. This motivates further investigation of DART across model scales and domains. Future work could also explore adaptive trace mining throughout post-training, dynamically targeting problems that remain challenging as model capabilities evolve.

7 Conclusion

We introduced DART, a trace-mining method that revisits uncertain reasoning steps in rejected traces and uses reference-answer guidance and a meta-thought to construct alternative candidates. DART improves MATH-500 recovery over matched step-level MC sampling, with ablations showing gains even without reference-answer guidance. Across the studied mathematical datasets, DART recovers problems missed by full-trace MC sampling, without a learned critic or process reward model.

On the 6,200 greedy-unsolved DeepMath-103K problems in the generation-cost analysis, DART recovers 37% more problems at nearly the same estimated generation cost per recovered problem and 30% lower cost per accepted trace. SFT on the resulting training corpora yields higher point estimates than MC sampling in all six evaluations and ranks first in five, supporting the practical value of DART for mining post-training data. These findings establish targeted exploration of rejected traces as a promising way to expand the supply of accepted traces for post-training.

Appendix A Reasoning step decomposition

Given a trace 𝐭\mathbf{t}, the decomposition procedure is:

  1. (i)

    Scan left to right and form text fragments at ., !, or ? followed by whitespace or the end of the trace, and at line breaks. Delimiters and whitespace remain attached to the original text.

  2. (ii)

    Initialize the annotation with [STEP]. After appending each text fragment to the annotated prefix, greedily decode a single token from the decomposition prompt below.

  3. (iii)

    If the decoded token opens a [STEP] marker, close the accumulated reasoning step and insert the marker into the annotated prefix; otherwise append the next text fragment to the same reasoning step. Stop requesting boundary decisions after the configured number of closed reasoning steps or at the end of the trace, and retain any remaining text as the final reasoning step.

The decoded token is used only as a boundary decision. Each reasoning step 𝐬j\mathbf{s}^{j} is assembled from substrings of the input, so concatenation reconstructs 𝐭\mathbf{t} exactly. The implementation batches decisions at the same fragment index across traces. Post-training runs allow ten closed reasoning steps plus any remaining suffix; the final reasoning step is not eligible for selection. The annotation markers are not included in the training corpora.

A.1 Prompt

The decomposition prompt 𝐩AUG\mathbf{p}_{\texttt{AUG}} is combined with the fixed demonstration below and the trace to annotate. The incremental procedure exposes only rule-based fragment boundaries and retains the original text regardless of the boundary decision.

We use the following demonstration throughout the experiments:

The following is a rejected greedy trace 𝐭AUG\mathbf{t}_{\texttt{AUG}} generated and decomposed by Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct for a random problem from the OpenMathInstruct-2 dataset. Decomposing this trace based on simple rules such as line breaks would result in incomplete reasoning steps, whereas the model is capable of decomposing it into self-contained steps, using the decomposition prompt 𝐩AUG\mathbf{p}_{\texttt{AUG}} from above:

Appendix B Reasoning step selection

The analysis in Figure 2 asks whether a ranking rule places useful alternative candidates early. For each rejected greedy trace from MATH-500, we generate one alternative candidate and its completed trace at every non-final reasoning step, without imposing a step budget. We then retrospectively rank the reasoning steps according to each selection score and measure the rank of the first accepted trace. This isolates selection from proposal generation.

The compared scores use greedy negative log-likelihood (G-NLL), inverse geometric mean token probability (PPL), the least probable token (MAX), reasoning step position alone (POS), or model self-reported confidence (LLM). Likelihood-based scores quantify local uncertainty (Aichberger et al., 2026; Fadeeva et al., 2023); position weighting favors earlier reasoning steps. The subscript POS denotes division by the one-indexed position jj, with larger scores ranked first. The displayed LLM score uses confidence elicited with the reference answer.

The analysis is restricted to problems with both accepted and rejected completed traces (125 problems). If every completed trace of a problem is rejected, the rank of the first accepted trace is undefined; if every one is accepted, all scores yield rank one and cannot be distinguished. The mean rank is therefore conditional on recovery being possible in the recorded set, not an expected cost over all greedy-unsolved problems. It counts alternative candidates, not model calls, tokens, or wall-clock time.

Appendix C Reasoning step diversity sampling

C.1 Prompt

DART and its three ablations in Section 2.3 (Figure 3) share the diversity prompt 𝐩DIV\mathbf{p}_{\texttt{DIV}} shown below. The prompt encourages the model to generate a self-contained alternative candidate 𝐬ALTj,r\mathbf{s}^{j,r}_{\texttt{ALT}} that follows the retained prefix 𝐬<j\mathbf{s}^{<j} and uses a different reasoning strategy from the selected reasoning step 𝐬j\mathbf{s}^{j}. Blue text provides the reference answer and instructions for using it (w/ sol). Green text requests a meta-thought before the alternative candidate (w/ rsn). Removing either or both components gives the three ablations. The <thought> and <alternative_step> tags are used to extract the meta-thought and alternative candidate from the generated output. The displayed prompt corresponds to the first proposal. For subsequent proposals at the same position, the selected reasoning step and all previously generated alternative candidates are included as separate <current_step> blocks, and the instruction asks for an alternative candidate that differs from all of them. This changing context enables different proposals even at T=0T=0.

C.2 Example

Consider the problem: given sin⁡(a+b)=3/5\sin(a+b)=3/5 and cos⁡(a+b)=4/5\cos(a+b)=4/5, find tan⁡((a+b)/2)\tan((a+b)/2). The reference answer is 1/31/3. The example below shows Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct replacing the initial reasoning step 𝐬1\mathbf{s}^{1} of the rejected trace in Section A.2 with the first alternative candidate 𝐬ALT1,1\mathbf{s}^{1,1}_{\texttt{ALT}}, then generating the continuation 𝐜1,1\mathbf{c}^{1,1}. The meta-thought guides the proposal but is excluded from the completed trace.

C.3 Ablation

Figure 6 extends Figure 3 from one to four alternative candidates per selected reasoning step, with one completed trace per alternative candidate. At four alternative candidates, DART covers 394 problems, including 224 greedy-solved problems, compared with 372 for step-level MC sampling with greedy continuation. The difference is 22 recovered problems, or 14.9% more recoveries among greedy-unsolved problems. Full-trace MC sampling with the largest displayed number of traces covers 417 problems but still misses some recovered by DART. The ablation therefore supports complementary coverage, not dominance at arbitrary budgets.

Appendix D Human and model-adjusted difficulty

Model-adjusted strata.

Difficulty levels 1 through 8 use the inclusive ranges [135,512][135,512], [85,133][85,133], [52,83][52,83], [32,50][32,50], [17,30][17,30], [7,15][7,15], [1,4][1,4], and {0}\{0\} for the number of accepted traces among 512 independently sampled traces, given by 512​q^​(𝐱)512\widehat{q}(\mathbf{x}) (Equation 4). These ranges were selected to obtain approximately equally sized difficulty strata. The implementation traverses aligned records of DART and MC sampling in stored order and retains up to the first 255 greedy-unsolved problems in each range. The methods are compared on identical strata, not on every greedy-unsolved problem. This subsampling affects neither trace generation nor post-training.

For a budget of kk completed traces, MC sampling uses entries 401 through 400+k400+k of the same ordered pool used to estimate q^​(𝐱)\widehat{q}(\mathbf{x}). It is therefore conditional on the pool defining each stratum. In particular, by construction, MC sampling recovers no problem in the stratum without accepted traces. An independent difficulty-estimation pool would be needed to evaluate recovery without this dependence.

Figures 8 and 9 extend Figure 4 to one, two, or four selected reasoning steps and one, two, or four alternative candidates per reasoning step. Their combinations yield budgets up to k=16k=16, with one completed trace per alternative candidate. Blue shades separate recoveries by the first selected reasoning step that yields an accepted trace. The adjacent bar separates overlap with MC sampling from method-specific recoveries.

Human-oriented labels.

Figure 7 groups the DeepMath-103K subset by its GPT-4o annotations based on Art of Problem Solving (AoPS) guidelines. The number of greedy-solved problems is not monotone in the assigned level: levels 8–9 contain more than levels 5–7 in this subset. These counts depend on the number of problems at each level and do not establish a reversal in per-problem success probability. Human-oriented curricular labels and the model-dependent quantity q𝜽​(𝐱)q_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}) serve different purposes. We use q^​(𝐱)\widehat{q}(\mathbf{x}) to describe recovery within the recorded pools of MC sampling.

Appendix E Generation-cost accounting

The analysis in Figure 5 estimates algorithmic matrix-multiplication FLOPs rather than accelerator utilization or elapsed time. For method mm, let TmT_{m} denote the sum of recorded uncached prompt tokens and generated tokens, PmP_{m} the number of cache-aware causal token pairs, and ZmZ_{m} the number of vocabulary-head evaluations. For a cached prefix of length cc followed by an uncached prefill suffix of length uu, the prefill contributes c​u+u⁡(u+1)/2cu+u(u+1)/2 pairs. Generating dd reported tokens after a prompt of length pp contributes p​d+d⁡(d+1)/2pd+d(d+1)/2 pairs. Thus, the telemetry convention treats every reported generated token as a decode-query position and can overcount transformer evaluations by one position per returned sequence. If one request returns multiple sequences, its first-token logits are shared; hence Zm=Gm−Sm+RmZ_{m}=G_{m}-S_{m}+R_{m}, where GmG_{m}, SmS_{m}, and RmR_{m} are the numbers of generated tokens, returned sequences, and requests, respectively.

For a dense gated decoder with LL layers, hidden width hh, intermediate width ff, query width dQd_{Q}, key/value width dK​Vd_{KV}, and vocabulary size VV, we compute

Fm=2​L​Tm​(h​dQ+2​h​dK​V+dQ​h+3​h​f)+4​L​dQ​Pm+2​h​V​Zm.\begin{split}F_{m}={}&2LT_{m}\bigl(hd_{Q}+2hd_{KV}+d_{Q}h+3hf\bigr)\\ &+4Ld_{Q}P_{m}+2hVZ_{m}.\end{split} (5)

The first term counts Q/K/V/O and gated-MLP projections, the second counts the query-key and attention-value products, and the third counts the vocabulary projection. We count each multiply-add as two FLOPs. For Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, L=32L=32, h=dQ=4,096h=d_{Q}=4{,}096, dK​V=1,024d_{KV}=1{,}024, f=14,336f=14{,}336, and V=128,256V=128{,}256. These dimensions give 13,958,643,712 projection and MLP FLOPs per model token, 524,288 attention FLOPs per causal token pair, and 1,050,673,152 FLOPs per vocabulary-head evaluation. Table 2 reports the resulting counters and estimates.

The estimate charges only uncached prompt queries while retaining the attention work of decoded queries over cached keys. It excludes embedding lookup, normalization, RoPE, nonlinear activations, softmax, sampling, padding, communication, verifier and CPU work, and any extra operations executed by a particular kernel implementation. The shared greedy generation, reasoning step decomposition, training, and evaluation are also outside the comparison. Consequently, Figure 5 estimates the dominant generation operations after reasoning step selection, not end-to-end runtime, energy, or hardware cost.

Appendix F Post-training protocol

Data.

We mine traces from 16,384 OpenMathInstruct-2 training problems or 8,192 DeepMath-103K training problems, filtering empty answers and exact duplicate problem strings. DeepMath-103K problems have annotated difficulty at least five. We evaluate on MATH-500 and the 2022–2025 American Invitational Mathematics Examinations (AIME) (Mathematical Association of America, 2022). No dedicated near-duplicate decontamination procedure was run beyond exact problem-string deduplication, so residual overlap or benchmark contamination cannot be excluded.

Trace mining.

All mining methods use Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Greedy traces use T=0T=0; MC sampling and RFT use T=1T=1. Reasoning traces are limited to 4,096 tokens, and generation uses a repetition penalty of 1.05. For DART, the procedure in Appendix A decomposes each rejected greedy trace, allowing ten closed reasoning steps plus any remaining suffix. We select up to four non-final reasoning steps and generate two alternative candidates per selected reasoning step. The meta-thought, alternative candidate, and continuation each use T=0T=0. Alternative candidates are generated sequentially, with earlier alternative candidates included in the next diversity prompt as described in Appendix C. The reference answer is provided to DART, STaR, and RFT prompts. Only accepted traces are retained, and accepted greedy traces are included in every training corpus. Meta-thoughts guide the proposals but are excluded from the training corpora.

Generation stages.

For each alternative candidate, DART generates a meta-thought, the alternative candidate itself, and a continuation. The meta-thought and alternative candidate can be generated jointly, and generation can be batched across reasoning steps and problems. Retained prefixes are not decoded again, but their context can incur prefill work unless KV caches are reused. We conduct a dedicated generation-cost analysis using a separately instrumented configuration (Appendix E).

Supervised fine-tuning.

Within each mining dataset, all runs start from the base checkpoint and use AdamW for two epochs, learning rate 10−510^{-5}, weight decay 0, 10% linear warm-up, effective batch size 128, maximum sequence length 4,096, and seed 42. The mining method determines the number and composition of retained traces; training corpora are not matched in examples or tokens.

Evaluation and intervals.

Greedy ∪\cup pass@kk counts an evaluation problem as solved if a separate greedy trace or at least one of kk stochastic traces is accepted. Stochastic traces are generated at T=1T=1. For each resampling draw, we select kk traces without replacement from each problem’s recorded pool and compute accuracy across the fixed evaluation set. We report the mean across draws and the central 95% empirical range. These intervals are conditional on the evaluation problems, recorded traces, and selected checkpoint; they do not resample problems or rerun generation or training. Table 1 uses k=32k=32 and reports the highest observed point estimate across evaluated checkpoints on each displayed evaluation set. These are exploratory, evaluation-selected results.

Sampling-budget curves.

Figure 10 reports Greedy ∪\cup pass@kk for post-training on OpenMathInstruct-2. Panel (10(a)) selects a checkpoint separately on each evaluation set. Panels (10(b)–10(d)) select one checkpoint per mining method using the named evaluation set, then evaluate it on all three sets. This distinguishes per-set checkpoint selection from cross-set evaluation of a fixed checkpoint; it does not remove the selection bias on the set used to choose that checkpoint.

Appendix G Broader impacts and existing assets

G.1 Broader impacts

DART improves the efficiency and coverage of reasoning-trace generation, supporting the development of more capable language models for mathematical reasoning and related tasks. However, final-answer verification does not guarantee the correctness of intermediate reasoning steps, and training on accepted traces may propagate such errors. More broadly, advances in reasoning capabilities may have implications beyond the mathematical domains studied here. Our experiments focus on mathematical reasoning and do not evaluate these broader effects.

G.2 Existing assets and licenses

Table 3 identifies the principal model and data assets, their roles, and the licenses stated by their maintainers. We cite both the MATH benchmark (Hendrycks et al., 2021) and the work introducing its 500-problem evaluation split (Lightman et al., 2024). Upstream repository licenses do not establish separate rights in all underlying competition content. In particular, the public Ai2 AIME dataset card does not state a license; we do not infer one from its public availability. AIME is used for evaluation, and no copy of this dataset is redistributed with the submission.

The implementation uses PyTorch (BSD-style), vLLM (Apache 2.0), Ray (Apache 2.0), and DeepSpeed (Apache 2.0). Hugging Face’s Transformers, Datasets, TRL, and Math-Verify each use Apache 2.0. The links credit the software projects and provide their license texts. We do not redistribute these packages, source datasets, generated training corpora, or model checkpoints with the submission.
